title: Digital identity is becoming an infrastructure layer for finance, work, public services, and age assurance, while trust and access remain use-case specific
source_unit: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology / Office for Digital Identities and Attributes, Digital Identity Sectoral Analysis Report 2026
geography: United Kingdom digital-identity sector and UK residents aged 18–66 in a weighted November 2025 consumer survey

denominator.unit: firms identified as providing digital-identity products and services in the UK

sector_gva.unit: million pounds estimated gross value added

provider_use_cases.value: 75% of providers offer identity or attribute verification; healthcare and public-service customers rose from 58% to 72% of firms reporting such customers

mechanism.value: Identity verification is moving from a niche compliance function toward a cross-sector infrastructure layer spanning finance, work, healthcare, public services, and age assurance

observations.method: Market taxonomy and firm-level assessment using company research, web data, audited accounts, Companies House filings, provider review, and modeled allocation across diversified firms.
observations.uncertainty: Revenue, GVA, and employment are estimates rather than a formal national-accounts series; the sector lacks a dedicated Standard Industrial Classification and the report does not establish policy causality.
observations.subgroup: UK digital-identity providers, customers, use cases, and sector segments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Market growth can reflect compliance demand, consolidation, or reclassification rather than broad consumer benefit or improved public-service access.

observations.period: November 2025 UK consumer survey; understanding and use of digital identity

denominator.unit: UK residents aged 18–66 surveyed by Survation; weighted by age, sex, region, income, qualifications, employment, socioeconomic group, and ethnicity

some_understanding.unit: percent reporting at least some understanding of digital identity

used_digital_identity.unit: percent reporting use of a digital identity service for at least one purpose

income_understanding_gap.value: 72% of respondents in households under £19,999 reported some understanding versus 88% among households earning £40,000 or more

income_use_gap.value: 65% of respondents in households under £19,999 reported use versus 87% among households earning £40,000 or more

mechanism.value: Digital identity familiarity and use are spreading, but income-linked gaps in understanding and use can turn identity infrastructure into a stratified access layer

observations.method: Weighted online consumer survey with updated use-case prompts and a larger sample than the 2025 baseline.
observations.uncertainty: The report warns that the revised questionnaire, expanded use cases, and changed baseline validation limit direct year-over-year comparison; self-reported use may include identity checks respondents did not recognize as such.
observations.subgroup: UK residents by age, household income, digital skills, digital access, and other demographic characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower reported use may reflect fewer life events requiring verification rather than exclusion, and awareness can improve without producing control over data or service choice.

observations.period: November 2025 UK consumer survey; context-specific digital versus physical preference

denominator.unit: weighted UK consumer survey respondents; scenario preferences are reported among the survey sample

online_age_purchase.value: 39% prefer digital identity and 25% prefer physical identity for online age-restricted purchases

public_services.value: 36% prefer digital and 28% physical for accessing government or NHS services

healthcare.value: 28% prefer digital and 35% physical for healthcare appointments

in_person_age.value: 23% prefer digital and 41% physical for proving age in a bar, restaurant, or cinema

mechanism.value: Acceptance of digital identity depends on the social and institutional context: convenience is more attractive online, while physical proof remains preferred in many embodied or sensitive encounters

observations.method: Scenario-based survey question offering digital, physical, either, would-not-do, and don't-know response options.
observations.uncertainty: Stated preference is not actual adoption, and scenarios differ in perceived risk, convenience, coercion, and ability to substitute one form of identity for another.
observations.subgroup: UK residents aged 18–66 across nine identity-verification scenarios.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may prefer physical identity in principle but still use digital identity when it is cheaper, faster, or required by a service; preference and practical choice can diverge.

observations.period: November 2025 UK consumer survey; importance, sentiment, and non-use

denominator.unit: weighted UK consumer survey respondents; non-use base is 1,307 respondents

future_importance.unit: percent saying digital identity will be important over the next five years

positive_direction.unit: percent with a very or somewhat positive view of the current direction of digital identity development

negative_direction.unit: percent with a very or somewhat negative view

non_user_reasons.value: Among non-users, 29% preferred physical ID, 29% had not needed to prove identity, 15% had no digital option, 15% were uncomfortable with the technology, and 12% cited privacy or security concerns

mechanism.value: People can expect digital identity to become important without positively endorsing its direction, creating a legitimacy problem in which inevitability is mistaken for consent

observations.method: Weighted survey measures of future importance, direction of development, and reasons for non-use; non-use reasons allow multiple responses.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not measure actual consent, privacy outcomes, coercive switching, complaint remedy, or the effect of the proposed national digital-ID policy on trust.
observations.subgroup: UK residents overall and respondents who reported no prior digital-identity use.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived importance may reflect expectation of institutional rollout rather than support; non-use can reflect lack of exposure rather than resistance.

related_sources.claim: UK baseline digital-identity sector assessment used for bounded comparison.
Comparative public-sector digital-identity adoption and non-digital-channel companion source.

boundary: This record adds a UK route from digital-identity market expansion and service embedding through consumer understanding, income-linked use, context-specific preference, public legitimacy, and exclusion risk. It preserves modeled market estimates, weighted survey, revised-baseline, self-report, and non-causal boundaries; it does not establish that digital identity improves service access, privacy, fraud outcomes, or trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GOV.UK report reviewed for sector size, market adoption, use cases, survey frame, income and access differences, scenario preferences, non-use, sentiment, future importance, methodology changes, and limitations.
